thread.title: Spotify Makes a Solid Debut—Could It Go Higher?

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Spotify Makes a Solid Debut—Could It Go Higher?
text:
NEW YORK, NY - APRIL 03: People walk by the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) on the morning that the music streaming service Spotify begins trading shares at the NYSE on April 3, 2018 in New York City. Trading under the symbol SPOT, the Swedish company's losses grew to 1.235 billion euros ($1.507 billion) last year, its largest ever. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images) Illustration: Spencer Platt/Getty Images Not a bad start for shares of streaming music pioneer Spotify Technology ( SPOT ) on the New York Stock Exchange today.
Although the shares fizzled from their opening price of $165.90, closing down at $149.01,that's not the way to look at it, according to Gabelli & Co .’s John Tinker.
Tinker, who initiated coverage of the stock today with a Hold rating, tells me it priced at a 10% pop from where the stock was in the private market on the day of the investor presentation, March 15th, using the "reference price" of $132 this morning.
Today’s close is another 13% jump from that reference price. In effect, using Tinker's rough numbers, " you’ve had two 10% pops ,” likening those increases to the first-day "pop" that some companies have in a traditional IPO.
This is an unusual debut, in that Spotify itself was not selling any shares, sitting on $1.5 billion in cash and having no need . Hence, share sales were all to insiders.
Unless everyone who owned sat on their hands from the open of trading, waiting for a big pop, they made off pretty well in today’s selling relative to what they could have gotten in recent weeks in the private market.
Nice to be an insider "They managed it well," Tinker says of the offering: nothing "left on the table" as far as the company is concerned, but those two pops were a nice payoff for the selling shareholders.
There's a particularly large concentration of insider ownership, with co-founder, CEO and chairman Daniel Ek holding just under 26% of the stock, and co-founder and board member Martin Lorentzon holding 13%.
Shares likely keep rising The stock is “ more likely to go up from here than down , and certainly not likely to go down that much,” concludes Tinker.
There is limited supply of shares, given the company is not itself selling shares. And there’s sure to be solid demand, he reckons, given institutional buyers probably now have to buy it.
“You have no float” in Spotify shares, Tinker says, “And the only people who couldn’t buy until today are institutions, most of whom can’t buy private stocks."
“Now, if you’re an institutional growth investor, you need to be in growth stocks. If you’re a big institution, you gotta own some of this."
All the more so given that, as Tinker points out, the preferred growth stocks have collapsed .
“ Facebook ( FB ) has been drifting, it’s market cap is now just $374 billion! And then let’s throw in Apple ( AAPL ), at $854 billion, and Amazon ( AMZN ) has collapsed and is still at $676 billion. You’re probably as an institution in these stocks already, but they’re no longer giving you the stock momentum.
“You add it up, and there’s gonna be some demand” for Spotify, he says.
Unlikely to change all IPOs Will Spotify's unusual offering change the IPO process? It seems unlikely. The terms are so different, the lack of float, the giant consumer brand name. It doesn't seem that every private unicorn can replicate this kind of audacious debut.
Will Spotify raise money at some point? A question for a little down the road is whether Spotify will decide it does need to raise capital. With all that cash, it doesn’t seem like it would need to anytime soon, so what could make the company do that?
“I don’t think they’ll run out of cash for quite a while,” says Tinker, but then, after a beat, he adds that Spotify is competing against Apple and Amazon for music audiences. “You can’t slow down” if you’re Spotify, he muses. Spotify might have to spend to find more customers. That’s because they have big barriers to entry. The service is popular and growing fast. But Apple Music has been growing fast as well — faster than Spotify, Apple would claim. And Amazon, says Tinker, “has woken up to how much fun music is” as a result of its “ Echo ” home appliance.
That might prompt Spotify to spend more money to find more customers, especially to off-set churn .
“You've got to find the customer,” says Tinker. “And then they churn out, and because your gross margin is so low [at Spotify], you don't have that many dollars to play with."
One possible route Spotify could go to is to amplify its service with its own hardware offering , like Amazon’s Echo. That would be a big new endeavor that could conceivably require more capital, as it would pressure Spotify’s already-low gross profit margin.
Spotify's hidden asset Tinker points out one last bit: The company owns 9% of Chinese media and messing giant Tencent Holding 's ( 0700HK ) " Tencent Music ," which is a comparable streaming service in China. Tencent, says Tinker, appears to have a lock on the China music streaming market, with perhaps 80% of the audience using its service.
That stake, valued at $1 billion, could become more valuable over time for Spotify. He likens it to another China asset that became a big deal not so long ago. "I’m dating myself, but remember when Yahoo! was a real company, and they owned this big stake in Alibaba [Group Holding ( BABA )]?"
"That would be like a hidden asset" for Spotify, he says. "It's a neat hedge" for the company.
